title: The Pecking Order of Culture, Strategy, and Talent
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The post takes up the perennial debate over whether culture, strategy or talent matters most for organizational success. It sketches the case each camp makes: culture has recently dominated attention, consultants favor strategy, and talent is what executes. The author's answer is that all three matter equally and depend on one another. Three corporate cases make the point by subtraction: Enron lacked culture, Circuit City lacked talent, and Polaroid lacked strategy. The best leaders therefore invest in all three, likened to a three-legged stool.
points: Rather than ranking culture, strategy and talent, the post argues they are equally important and interdependent.
Each is incomplete alone: culture without talent spins its wheels, and talent without strategy is a fast ship in a choppy sea.
Enron, Circuit City and Polaroid each illustrate failure from the missing leg.
Leaders should hold themselves accountable for selecting talent, setting strategy and building culture together.
quotes: Without the talent to execute, however, a positive culture spins its wheels. If, as it has been famously said, culture eats strategy for lunch, then talent sets the table.
Talent without strategy, they will tell you, is a fast ship in a choppy sea.
It’s time to recognize that all three matter equally and are highly interdependent. When any one component is missing, the others lose their way.
Never forget the lesson of Enron: Talent and strategy without culture produced a nightmare of ambition and an unethical food fight of untold mischief.
Or the lesson of Polaroid: Culture and talent without strategy allowed technology and competitors to destroy one of the most successful organizations in the history of business.
They hold themselves accountable to selecting superior talent, setting a compelling strategy, and creating a high-performance culture.
